title: BMS and the 12 February 2026 strike
author: Editorial Desk
summary: BMS stated that it would not participate and explained why.
body:
*Photo: BMS statement on the 12 February 2026 strike*

A general strike by several central trade unions has been called for 12 February 2026. On 31 January 2026, Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) issued a statement saying that it neither supports the strike nor will take part in it, and calling it politically motivated. This post sets out what BMS said, the reasons it gave, what it wants instead, and the view of those who called the strike, so that readers can see both sides before the day.

## What the BMS statement says

According to the BMS press statement of 31 January, the strike has been called for political motives by certain central trade unions together with the Samyukta Kisan Morcha, a farmers' platform. BMS says that political interests should be kept out of the labour sector. Its General Secretary, Ravindra Himte, was quoted in the press as saying that BMS consistently supports constructive and pro-labour initiatives of the Government, while it continues to object to policies it believes could harm workers.

The statement is also a statement about the Labour Codes. BMS says that it welcomes the four Labour Codes, that it considers the Code on Wages and the Code on Social Security historic and revolutionary, and that it has concerns about provisions in two of the four Codes. It mentions two meetings with the Union Labour Minister, on 13 and 21 November 2025, at which, according to BMS, the Minister assured it that the Government would address its concerns. On the strength of those assurances, BMS welcomed the notifications that brought the Codes into force on 21 November.

## The background: the Codes and a divided trade union movement

To understand why one union stays away while others strike, it helps to recall what happened in the last quarter of 2025. On 21 November the Government brought all four Labour Codes into force, consolidating 29 central labour laws. The Government's announcement said that they provide appointment letters for all workers, minimum wages for all workers, a national floor wage, social security for gig and platform workers, and gratuity after one year for fixed-term employees.

Trade unions did not react in the same way. On the day of implementation, a BMS delegation met the Labour Minister and submitted a memorandum which supported the Codes on Wages and Social Security but opposed certain provisions of the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code. On 16 December, sixteen central trade unions, including BMS, stated at a summit in New Delhi that they supported the Codes and would work to spread awareness of them. Other central unions have said that the Codes favour employers and weaken workers' rights, and they have called for protest, including the strike on 12 February.

## What BMS wants instead

BMS has reiterated its own demands, which it says it has been raising directly with the Government. In its memorandum of 21 November 2025, it asked for:

- Convening of the Indian Labour Conference, which has not met since 2016, and which all central unions have long sought.
- Raising of the EPF wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000, of the ESI limit from Rs 21,000 to Rs 42,000, and of the bonus calculation ceiling from Rs 7,000 to Rs 14,000.
- A minimum pension of Rs 7,500 in place of Rs 1,000, linked to the Consumer Price Index, with health cover under Ayushman Bharat.
- Higher honoraria for Anganwadi workers and helpers, ASHA workers, mid-day meal workers and other scheme workers.
- Regularisation of long-term contract workers in central government establishments and public sector undertakings.
- Budgetary compensation for welfare boards, such as the beedi board, whose cess-based funding was removed after GST.

The statement of 31 January refers in particular to implementation of the Wage and Social Security Codes, social security for unorganised workers, the minimum pension and the regularisation of scheme workers. These are demands that, in BMS's view, are best pursued through talks and tripartite consultation.

## The reasons offered

BMS's reasoning can be set out in three points:

- It regards the call as part of a political opposition to the Government's policies and not primarily as a response to workers' interest. Its test in such cases is whether the action is about workers or about a party's agenda.
- It prefers talks and tripartite consultation, and says that the Labour Minister has given assurances that its concerns will be addressed.
- It says that the Codes include provisions beneficial to workers, and that corrections to the others should be sought through discussion, not stoppage.

These reasons are consistent with the method that BMS has described for years: dialogue first and agitation as a last resort. A similar position was taken in May 2025, when BMS declined to join a Bharat Bandh against the Labour Codes, also calling it politically motivated. BMS has not, however, stayed away from all strikes in its history; accounts of its past record that it joined the 1974 general strike and protests against changes in labour law in 2014.

## The other side

The unions that called the strike say that the Codes weaken workers' rights, and that strikes are the way to resist. Their argument is that a worker's bargaining power depends on the ability to stop work, and that the Codes, by extending notice and conciliation rules and by recognising fixed-term employment, give employers more room. They also argue that gains such as those promised on social security will mean little without proper enforcement. They reject the label of "political". In their view, the issues are wages, job security and union rights, and these are of concern to workers whatever the party in power.

Readers should hear both views. It is not unusual in India for trade union movements to be divided by affiliation, and it is notable that on the Labour Codes the division runs across the movement and not between workers and employers alone.

## The legal frame for any strike

Under the Industrial Relations Code, as summarised by PRS Legislative Research, a strike requires 14 days' prior notice, valid for up to 60 days, and is barred during conciliation and tribunal proceedings and for a period afterwards. Employees of Government are in addition subject to conduct rules. A call for a general strike therefore affects different workers differently, and the legal consequences of staying away from work vary with the sector and the employer.

## For observers: how to read the day

A strike's impact depends on how many sectors join and how long it lasts. A general strike is usually felt most in public sector undertakings, banks, transport and coal, where unions are strong and work stops are visible, and less in the large informal economy, where workers have no employer to notify and no wages to lose lightly. News reports and official statements often differ in their estimates, because organisers count participants differently from governments, and because turnout varies from State to State. It is wise to read more than one source, to distinguish claims from verified figures, and to look at what each side demands afterwards, not only on the day.

## A closing thought

The difference between BMS and the unions that are striking is not a difference about whether workers deserve better wages, pensions and security. All of them say they want that. It is a difference about method and about the reading of the Codes: whether the way forward is through dialogue with the Government while pressing for corrections, or through a collective show of strength. The issues that BMS has listed, a minimum pension that reflects the cost of living, a fair honorarium for scheme workers, social security that actually reaches the unorganised worker, will remain whatever happens on 12 February. They are the real test of whether any reform has reached the worker.
